stimulus.text:
| City | Region | Approximate population at its height |
| Tenochtitlan (Mexica) | Central Mexico | About 200,000 |
| Cahokia (Mississippian) | Mississippi River valley, near present-day St. Louis | About 20,000 |
stimulus.source_note: Approximate figures; Cahokia about 20,000 at its peak in the 1200s and Tenochtitlan about 200,000, consistent with standard estimates (see grounding).

stem: A historian argues that food production, more than any other factor, determined how complex a Native American society became. Which comparison would provide the strongest test of this argument?

options.text: Comparing a maize-farming chiefdom with a non-farming foraging society in the same environment.
Comparing two maize-farming societies that lived in very different regions of the Americas.
options.misconception: Tests region, not farming, since both societies in the pair farm.

options.text: Comparing the religious ceremonies and rituals of Mexica and Inca peoples.
options.misconception: Tests religion, which is not the factor the argument names.

options.text: Comparing European metal tools with the stone tools used by Native peoples.
options.misconception: Tests tools, which is not the factor the argument names.

rationales.A: Same environment, different food production: the comparison holds other things steady and isolates the factor in question.
rationales.B: Both societies in this pair farm, so the comparison cannot test whether farming itself is decisive.
rationales.C: Religious ceremonies test religion, not food production, so they cannot test this argument.
rationales.D: Tools test technology, not food production, so they cannot test this argument.
rationales.general:
1. Name the claim. Food production decided how complex a society became.
2. Ask what would test it. Change food production and hold the rest steady, like a lab test with one variable.
3. Build the pair. A maize-farming chiefdom and a non-farming foraging society in the same environment differ in food alone.
4. Check the other pairs. Two farming societies, two religions, or two tool kits all test something else.
Remember: to test one cause, compare cases that differ in that cause alone.
